seo_title: Solar Marketing in South Delhi: Premium Homes Guide
description: Solar marketing in South Delhi: how installers can position for kothis, builder floors and farmhouses, qualify big-bill homes and book more site visits.
headline: Solar marketing in South Delhi: selling to kothis, builder floors and farmhouses
card_text: How installers can win high-value rooftop projects in South Delhi's colonies and farmhouse belts: premium positioning, builder-floor roof rights and site visits that close.
intro:
Solar marketing in South Delhi is a different job from selling rooftop solar anywhere else in the city. The homes are larger, the electricity bills are higher, and many owners have already been called by three national brands before you reach them. A household running several ACs, a lift, a pump and sometimes an EV charger is not shopping for the cheapest 3 kW system. It wants a contractor it trusts on a terrace it cares about.

This guide is for installers and EPCs who want more of those projects in colonies such as Greater Kailash, Defence Colony, Vasant Vihar, Panchsheel, Hauz Khas and Safdarjung Enclave, and in the farmhouse belts of Chhatarpur, Sainik Farms and Westend. It covers who buys, which Delhi rules matter for big systems, and how to turn premium enquiries into booked site visits.

sections.h2: Who buys rooftop solar in South Delhi
sections.html:
South Delhi mixes four very different kinds of buyer. If your ads and sales process treat them all the same, you'll pay for leads you can't close.

BuyerTypical areasWho decidesWhat they care about
Kothi or bungalow ownerVasant Vihar, Westend, Anand Lok, Shanti NiketanThe family, often after an architect or manager weighs inLook of the structure, brands, warranty, who will maintain it
Builder floor ownersGreater Kailash, Defence Colony, Lajpat Nagar, Saket, Malviya NagarWhoever holds the terrace rights, sometimes all floor owners togetherRoof rights, who pays, how savings are split, leakage risk
Farmhouse ownerChhatarpur, Sainik Farms, Rajokri, Westend GreensOwner or estate managerLarge loads, ground-mounted or shed options, backup during outages
DDA and group housing flatsVasant Kunj, Sheikh Sarai, Saket, Sarita ViharRWA or managing committeeCommon-area bill savings, society subsidy, maintenance

Most of your margin sits in the first three rows. Flat owners will still fill in your forms, so ask about house type up front and route society enquiries into a separate committee pitch, as we describe in our guide to solar marketing in Dwarka.

sections.h2: Delhi rules that change the pitch for big homes
sections.html:
• The DISCOM is mostly BSES Rajdhani (BRPL). BRPL supplies most of South and West Delhi, so your quotes and landing page should explain BRPL's rooftop application and net-metering steps. A few pockets near the New Delhi area fall under NDMC, so always confirm from the customer's bill.
  • Subsidy is a small share of a large system. The Delhi Solar Portal lists a state capital subsidy of up to ₹26,000 per kW for the first 3 kW, capped at ₹78,000, and no additional state subsidy from 3 kW to 10 kW. The central PM Surya Ghar subsidy is also capped at 3 kW. On an 8–10 kW kothi system, subsidy helps, but it isn't why the customer buys.
  • The free route mostly won't apply. Delhi's September 2026 policy amendment offers up to 3 kW at zero upfront cost to eligible households using up to 400 units a month. A South Delhi home with a ₹15,000+ summer bill is usually well above that, which is exactly why it is a paying vendor-route customer.
  • Size against sanctioned load. Big homes often have a sanctioned load that hasn't kept pace with their ACs. Check the bill and the current DERC net-metering rules before you propose a size, and tell the customer early if a load enhancement is needed.

Rules and amounts change. Check the Delhi Solar Portal, the PM Surya Ghar portal and BRPL before you put a figure in an ad, and follow the wording in our guide to PM Surya Ghar subsidy ads.

sections.h2: Premium positioning: lead with design, not discount
sections.html:
In South Delhi, a "lowest price" or "free solar" message pulls in the wrong people and puts off the right ones. Owners who spend on interiors and landscaping judge an installer by how the terrace will look and who will be accountable later. Build your marketing around that:

  1. Show the structure. Elevated structures that leave the terrace usable for gatherings, neat cable routing and clean railings are a selling point here. Photograph them well.
  2. Name the components. List panel, inverter and structure brands, warranty terms and who honours them. Vague "tier-1 panels" copy reads as cheap.
  3. Make service visible. Explain cleaning schedules, monitoring on the owner's phone and response times for faults.
  4. Offer a proper proposal. A shade analysis, a layout drawing and a year-one generation estimate with assumptions stated beats a WhatsApp price list.
  5. Talk to the advisers. Architects, interior designers and estate managers often influence the decision. A one-page brief they can forward helps.

sections.h2: Builder floors: solve the roof-rights question first
sections.html:
Much of Greater Kailash, Defence Colony, Lajpat Nagar and nearby colonies has been rebuilt as builder floors, with three or four owners in one plot. The top-floor owner or the original plot owner often holds the terrace rights, and the other owners may object to anything installed there.

  • Ask in the lead form: "Do you have terrace rights, or will other floor owners need to agree?"
  • Offer clear options: a system for the rights-holder's connection only, or separate systems for more than one floor where the roof and the rules allow it. Explain the trade-offs plainly.
  • Give the owners something to share. A short PDF covering roof loading, waterproofing, space used and each owner's expected saving helps the family or neighbours agree.

Leads that answer "other owners need to agree" aren't bad leads. They need a longer follow-up track, so tag them in your CRM instead of dropping them.

sections.h2: Ads and local search for South Delhi
sections.html:
• Target colonies, not "Delhi". On Meta, use pin-drop radiuses around the colonies and farmhouse belts you serve. On Google, target the same areas and bid on searches such as "solar panel installation South Delhi", "rooftop solar Greater Kailash", "solar for farmhouse Delhi" and "10 kW solar system price Delhi".
  • Qualify on bill, not just interest. Ask for the average monthly bill or units, house type, terrace rights and colony. Higher-intent forms get fewer leads, but in South Delhi they usually waste less sales time.
  • Use creatives that match the audience. A walk-through of a finished terrace, an owner explaining their bill before and after (with permission) and a calm explainer on system sizing work better than countdown offers.
  • Add negatives such as jobs, course, training, franchise, dealership and "free solar" so your budget goes to buyers.
  • Win Maps for your base area. Keep your Google Business Profile updated with South Delhi project photos, and ask customers to mention their colony in reviews.

For DISCOM-level targeting across the rest of the city, see solar lead generation in Delhi.

sections.h2: Site visits that close high-value projects
sections.html:
A premium enquiry is often lost at the site visit, not in the ad. A few habits make a big difference:

  1. Reply fast and properly. Call within 10 minutes during working hours, then send a WhatsApp message with your name, company, a past project nearby and a request for the latest BRPL bill.
  2. Send a senior person. The owner will ask about load, structure height and warranty on the terrace. A junior surveyor who can't answer loses trust.
  3. Plan for the colony. Many South Delhi colonies have gated entry and guards. Confirm the visitor's name with the owner so your team gets in on time.
  4. Leave with a date. Agree when the written proposal will arrive, and present it on a call rather than just sending a PDF.
  5. Follow up for weeks. Big systems take family discussions. A planned sequence of three or four useful messages works better than repeated "any update?" calls.

sections.h2: Solar marketing in South Delhi: what to measure
sections.html:
Judge channels by cost per site visit and cost per kW sold, not by cost per form fill. In South Delhi, a campaign with fewer, larger projects can beat one with twice the leads.

MetricWhy it matters here
Share of leads above your bill thresholdShows whether targeting is reaching big-bill homes
Lead to site visit rateTests your speed of reply and first-call quality
Average system size soldTells you whether premium positioning is working
Cost per kW sold by channelLets you compare Meta, Google, Maps and referrals fairly

For reference, our rooftop solar campaigns run at ₹60–80 per qualified enquiry when they're working well, and at scale our solar clients typically get 20–30 leads a day and 5–10 site visits a week. A premium South Delhi campaign may trade volume for larger projects, and results always depend on budget, area and follow-up.

faqs: Which DISCOM serves South Delhi for rooftop solar net metering?

Most of South Delhi is supplied by BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (BRPL). A few pockets near the New Delhi area are served by NDMC, so confirm the DISCOM and sanctioned load from the customer's latest bill before you size a system.
Is there a subsidy for a 10 kW rooftop solar system in South Delhi?

Subsidy is linked to the first 3 kW. The Delhi Solar Portal lists up to ₹26,000 per kW for the first 3 kW, capped at ₹78,000, with no additional state subsidy from 3 kW to 10 kW, and the central PM Surya Ghar subsidy is also capped at 3 kW. Check both portals for current rules before you quote.
How can a solar installer get leads from South Delhi kothis and farmhouses?

Target the colonies and farmhouse belts you serve with Meta and Google ads, qualify leads on monthly bill, house type and terrace rights, show high-quality photos of finished terraces, and send a senior person to the site visit with a proper proposal.
Can builder floor owners in South Delhi install rooftop solar?

Often yes, but terrace rights matter. The owner who holds the terrace rights usually needs to agree, and other floor owners may need to as well. Installers should ask about roof rights in the first conversation and explain the options for one or more connections.
